prompt: Should students be required to learn a second language? Write an essay taking a position.
text:
# Why Every Student Should Learn a Second Language

Students should be required to learn a second language. The benefits reach well beyond the classroom, and the cost of requiring it is small compared with what students gain.

The strongest argument is cognitive. Learning a language asks the brain to hold two systems of words and grammar at once and to switch between them. Research on bilingual people has linked this practice to stronger attention, better memory, and a delay in the onset of age-related decline. These findings are debated in some details, but the broad pattern is hard to ignore. Language study is mental exercise that students cannot easily get elsewhere.

A second language also teaches students about their first. Many English speakers never think about grammar until they must learn how another language handles verbs or word order. Then they begin to see how their own language works. This awareness improves their writing and their ability to explain ideas clearly.

The practical case is just as strong. The world is more connected than ever, and employers value workers who can talk to customers and partners in more than one language. Even in jobs where language skills are not required, they set a candidate apart. For a student who plans to travel, study abroad, or work internationally, a second language is a direct advantage.

There is also a human reason. Learning a language means learning how other people think, joke, and describe the world. A student who studies Spanish, Mandarin, or Arabic gains a way into another culture that translation cannot fully offer. This builds empathy and curiosity, which societies need more of.

Critics raise fair objections. Some say school time is limited and should go to math, science, and reading. Others point out that many adults took years of language classes and still cannot hold a conversation. Both concerns are real, but they argue for better teaching, not for dropping the requirement. Schools can start language study in the early grades, when children learn most easily. They can focus on speaking and listening instead of memorizing word lists. They can also let students choose among several languages, so that the work feels relevant to them.

A requirement matters because without one, the opportunity goes mostly to students from well-funded schools and families. If language study is optional, those who most need new opportunities are the least likely to get them. Making it standard gives every student the same chance.

In short, a second language sharpens the mind, strengthens understanding of one's own language, opens career doors, and builds respect for other cultures. Schools should require it and then work to teach it well.
